name: terminal
description: Execute one shell command inside the workspace. The most powerful and least constrained tool in this set — it can read, write, install, delete, or reach the network — and is scoped by policy and confirmation rather than by a narrow schema the way the read-only tools are.

command.description: The literal command line to execute. Never assembled by concatenating untrusted or user-supplied text into a larger string — see `safety_notes`.

description.description: One plain-language sentence describing what this command does, shown to the human approving it. Required, because 'run this command' with no description is not something a person can meaningfully consent to.

cwd.description: Working directory the command runs from, relative to the workspace root. Must resolve inside the workspace root.

timeout_ms.description: Hard ceiling on execution time. A command that has not finished when this elapses is terminated and `timed_out` is reported true — a runtime with no timeout can hang a whole session on one stuck process.

exit_code.description: Process exit code. Null if the process was terminated before exiting on its own — see `timed_out`.

stdout.description: Captured standard output. May be truncated for an unusually long-running or noisy command; a truncated capture is marked, never silently cut.

stderr.description: Captured standard error, kept separate from `stdout` so a caller can tell diagnostic noise from the command's actual output.

timed_out.description: True if `timeout_ms` was reached and the process was terminated rather than finishing on its own.

errors.description: The human declined to run this command. Reported as a first-class outcome, never retried automatically and never silently reattempted under a different description.
`cwd` resolves outside the workspace root and was refused before the command was ever spawned.
The command could not be started at all — e.g. the interpreter or binary named does not exist on this machine.

safety_notes: This is the one tool in this set that can mutate anything, so it carries obligations the read-only four do not: `requires_confirmation` is always true and may never be bypassed by a caller regardless of how routine the command appears; `command` must be built only from literal, known-safe segments — never by interpolating text a human did not explicitly write, since that is the direct path to command injection; every invocation must carry a real `timeout_ms` rather than relying on the default silently; and a destructive or hard-to-reverse command (deleting files, force-pushing, resetting state) should be named as such in `description` so the approval it requests is an informed one, not a formality. When a read-only tool in this set (`read_file`, `list_directory`, `search_workspace`, `git_status`) can answer the same question, it should be preferred over `terminal` — see `skills/reasoning.md`.
